claim: Malaria caused an estimated 405,000 deaths in 2018, most attributable to Plasmodium falciparum.
source: In 2018, malaria was estimated to have caused 405,000 deaths, most of them attributable to the virulent Plasmodium falciparum parasite species (World Health Organization, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization 2019 report.

claim: Artemisinin-based Combination Therapies (ACTs) have been the recommended first-line therapy for P. falciparum infection since 2001.
source: Since 2001, Artemisinin-based Combination Therapies (ACTs) have been the recommended first-line therapy for P. falciparum infection for almost all malaria-endemic areas (World Health Organization, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization 2001 report.

claim: ACTs have contributed to a major reduction in malaria-related mortality and morbidity.
source: These treatments have contributed to a major reduction in malaria-related mortality and morbidity (Eastman and Fidock, 2009; Carrara et al., 2006; Bhatt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: The first instances of reduced artemisinin efficacy were described in western Cambodia in 2008.
source: However, in 2008, the first instances of reduced artemisinin efficacy were described in western Cambodia (Dondorp et al., 2009; Ashley et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: Artemisinin resistance has spread rapidly throughout Southeast Asia.
source: Subsequent studies have documented the rapid spread of resistance throughout Southeast Asia (Dondorp et al., 2009; Ashley et al., 2014; World Health Organization, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three sources.

claim: Artemisinin resistance is partial and affects only ring-stage parasites.
source: Resistance to artemisinin is partial and affects only rings (World Health Organization, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization 2018 report.

claim: Partial artemisinin resistance manifests clinically as a parasite clearance half-life exceeding 5.5 hours.
source: Clinically, this partial resistance trait manifests as a parasite clearance half-life that exceeds 5.5 hr (WWARN K13 Genotype-Phenotype Study Group, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the WWARN K13 Genotype-Phenotype Study Group 2019.

claim: The pfk13 gene on chromosome 13 is linked to artemisinin resistance.
source: An analysis of P. falciparum parasites selected for artemisinin resistance in vitro as well as parasites from patients experiencing slow parasite clearance led to the identification of a genetic locus linked to resistance: a kelch domain-containing protein located on chromosome 13 (pfk13) (Ariey et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ariey et al., 2014.

claim: Nine pfk13 missense mutations have been validated for artemisinin resistance: F446I, N458Y, M476I, Y493H, R539T, I543T, P553L, R561H and C580Y.
source: To date, many missense mutations have been described in the BTP/POZ or kelch propeller domain-containing parts of this protein in clinical isolates, however only nine of them have been validated for artemisinin resistance (F446I, N458Y, M476I, Y493H, R539T, I543T, P553L, R561H and C580Y) (World Health Organization, 2018; Ariey et al., 2014; Straimer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three sources.

claim: The pfk13 C580Y mutation is the most prevalent pfk13 variant in Southeast Asia.
source: In most locations, the pfk13 C580Y mutation has overtaken other resistance-inducing variants, and it is now the most prevalent pfk13 variant in Southeast Asia (Ashley et al., 2014; Ariey et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: South America has historically been a second hotspot outside Southeast Asia for the evolution of antimalarial drug resistance.
source: South America has historically been a second hotspot outside Southeast Asia for the evolution of antimalarial drug resistance.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Chloroquine and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine resistance evolved simultaneously in Southeast Asia and South America.
source: For example, chloroquine and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine resistance evolved simultaneously in both regions (Wootton et al., 2002; Roper et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: Mining activities in the Guiana Shield favor malaria transmission, particularly P. falciparum.
source: These mining activities favor malaria transmission, particularly P. falciparum (Douine et al., 2016; Heemskerk, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: In Guyana in 2010, 5.1% (5 out of 98) of P. falciparum-infected clinical samples exhibited the pfk13 C580Y mutation.
source: In Guyana in 2010, 5.1% (5 out of 98) of P. falciparum-infected clinical samples, sharing a common haplotype different from their Cambodian counterparts, exhibited the pfk13 C580Y mutation (Chenet et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chenet et al., 2016.

claim: The 2010 Guyana pfk13 C580Y samples shared a common haplotype different from Cambodian counterparts.
source: In Guyana in 2010, 5.1% (5 out of 98) of P. falciparum-infected clinical samples, sharing a common haplotype different from their Cambodian counterparts, exhibited the pfk13 C580Y mutation (Chenet et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chenet et al., 2016.

claim: A 2014 therapeutic efficacy study in Guyana with 50 patients failed to identify pfk13 mutations or delayed parasite clearance time after artemether/lumefantrine treatment.
source: The most recent therapeutic efficacy study conducted in Guyana in 2014 with 50 patients failed to identify pfk13 mutations or delayed parasite clearance time after artemether/lumefantrine treatment (Rahman et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rahman et al., 2016.

claim: Fourteen samples bearing the pfk13 C580Y variant were identified from 854 samples collected in Guyana between March 2016 and September 2017, representing a prevalence of 1.6%.
source: We genotyped the propeller domain of the pfk13 gene by Sanger sequencing 854 samples collected between March 2016 and September 2017 from different malaria-endemic regions of Guyana. Fourteen samples bearing the pfk13 C580Y variant were identified, representing a prevalence of 1.6% (CI950.8–2.5%).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study's genotyping results.

claim: The prevalence of pfk13 C580Y mutants was 8.8% in Region 1, 0.7% in Region 8, and 0.5% in Region 7 of Guyana.
source: The prevalence of mutants was 8.8% (CI953.6–14.0%) in Region 1, 0.7% (CI950.0–2.0%) in Region 8 and 0.5% (CI950.0–1.1%) in Region 7 (Figure 1, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the text and Figure 1.

claim: All samples bearing the pfk13 C580Y variant also exhibited the pfk13 K189T mutation.
source: All samples bearing the pfk13 C580Y variant also exhibited the pfk13 K189T mutation, which to date has not been associated with artemisinin resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study's genotyping results.

claim: The pfk13 K189T mutation has not been associated with artemisinin resistance.
source: All samples bearing the pfk13 C580Y variant also exhibited the pfk13 K189T mutation, which to date has not been associated with artemisinin resistance.
evidence: The claim is stated as current knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: The pfk13 C580Y variant in Guyana arose on a single Guyanese parasite genetic background and was not imported from Southeast Asia.
source: The variant profile observed in the sequenced samples identified that the pfk13 C580Y variant arose on a single Guyanese parasite genetic background, and was not imported from Southeast Asia (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data presented in Figure 2a.

claim: Guyanese pfk13 C580Y parasites show extremely high relatedness (IBD >0.77) to each other.
source: This analysis revealed an extremely high level of relatedness between sample pairs bearing pfk13 C580Y (identity by descent (IBD) >0.77) relative to pairwise comparisons containing at least one wild-type pfk13 sample (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by identity-by-descent analysis presented in Figure 2b.

claim: The pfk13 C580Y parasite lineage in Guyana engaged in limited sexual outcrossing with other parasite lineages despite persisting for sufficient time to be observed in multiple regions.
source: This indicates that the parasite lineage on which C580Y arose in Guyana in 2010 probably engaged in limited sexual outcrossing with other parasite lineages in Guyana, despite having persisted for a sufficient duration of time to be observed in multiple regions of the country and to have risen to a non-negligible frequency in the Region 1 population.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high IBD values among C580Y parasites.

claim: Only two low-quality single nucleotide variants were identified among the 13 pfk13 C580Y mutant samples in the 75 kb segments flanking the C580Y-coding variant.
source: In the 75 kb segments flanking the 2016–2017 C580Y-coding variant, WGS identified only two low-quality single nucleotide variants among the 13 mutant samples (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data.

claim: Two different pfk13 C580Y haplotypes were identified using eight microsatellite loci flanking the pfk13 gene, differing at one locus positioned at −6.36 kb.
source: We also analyzed pfk13 C580Y parasites using eight microsatellite loci flanking the pfk13 gene. Despite missing data for some loci in some samples, two different haplotypes were identified, differing at one locus positioned at −6.36 kb (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microsatellite analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: The most common 2016-2017 pfk13 C580Y haplotype matched the previously identified Guyana A mutant haplotype from 2010.
source: The previously identified Guyana A mutant haplotype (Chenet et al., 2016) matched the most common haplotype in the 2016–2017 samples, which was markedly distinct from the one observed in pfk13 Cambodian mutants (Chenet et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of microsatellite data with previously published data.

claim: The Guyana pfk13 C580Y haplotype is markedly distinct from the one observed in pfk13 Cambodian mutants.
source: The previously identified Guyana A mutant haplotype (Chenet et al., 2016) matched the most common haplotype in the 2016–2017 samples, which was markedly distinct from the one observed in pfk13 Cambodian mutants (Chenet et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of microsatellite data with Cambodian samples.

claim: A de novo microsatellite mutation likely occurred at locus −6.36 following the origin of the C580Y mutation.
source: As replicate genotyping efforts reproduced the allelic variant at locus −6.36, it is likely that a de novo microsatellite mutation occurred at locus −6.36 following the origin of the C580Y mutation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from replicate genotyping data showing a consistent variant.

claim: The high similarity of microsatellite haplotypes bearing C580Y between 2010 and 2016 suggests the chromosome 13 resistance haplotype has persisted over this timespan.
source: The high similarity of the microsatellite haplotypes bearing C580Y between 2010 (Chenet et al., 2016) and 2016 suggests that the chromosome 13 resistance haplotype, and perhaps the full clonal lineage, has persisted over this timespan, as several of the allelic markers associated with the C580Y mutation are rare in both studies (e.g. allele 277 at marker −6.36: 11%; allele 206 at marker −0.15: 9%; allele 244 at marker 72.3: 6% Chenet et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the persistence of rare allelic markers over time.

claim: None of the previously described Southeast Asian partner mutations associated with pfk13-mutant parasites were observed in Guyanese isolates.
source: None of the previously described mutations were observed, including the pffd D193Y, pfcrt N326S, pfcrt I356T, pfarps V127M and pfmdr2 T484I variants.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis comparing Guyanese and Southeast Asian parasites.

claim: The pfcrt gene in Guyanese parasites was of South American origin with a 7G8 haplotype comprising mutations C72S, K76T, A220S, N326D and I356L.
source: The pfcrt gene was of South American origin with a 7G8 haplotype comprising the mutations C72S, K76T, A220S, N326D and I356L, with no particular difference between wild-type and pfk13 C580Y parasites (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis data.

claim: Two fixed differences were observed between wild-type and pfk13 C580Y parasites within the gene PF3D7_1252100 (RON3).
source: However, within this candidate gene set, we observed two fixed differences between wild-type and pfk13 C580Y parasites, both within the gene PF3D7_1252100 (RON3) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis data.

claim: All genotyped pfk13 C580Y mutants (n = 5) contained a V1661L-coding variant in the RON3 gene.
source: Although overall genotyping rates were low in this gene (successful for 15 out of 53), all genotyped pfk13 C580Y mutants (n = 5) contained a V1661L-coding variant and all genotyped pfk13 wild-type parasites (n = 9) carried a synonymous non-reference variant at codon 1801.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis data.

claim: All pfk13 C580Y variants were pfcrt SVMNT (72-76)/A220S/N326D/C350/I356L, pfdhfr double-mutant (N51I/S108N), pfdhps triple-mutant (A437G/K540E/A581G) and pfmdr1 triple-mutant (Y184F/N1042D/D1246Y).
source: All pfk13 C580Y variants were pfcrt SVMNT (72-76)/A220S/N326D/C350/I356L (i.e. the pfcrt 7G8 haplotype), pfdhfr double-mutant (N51I/S108N), pfdhps triple-mutant (A437G/K540E/A581G) and pfmdr1 triple-mutant (Y184F/N1042D/D1246Y).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular marker analysis data.

claim: The highest prevalence of the Guyanese pfk13 C580Y variant was found in Region 1.
source: The highest prevalence of the Guyanese pfk13 C580Y variant was found in Region 1.
evidence: The claim is supported by prevalence data from the study.

claim: The pfk13 C580Y variant was first observed in Region 1 in April 2016 and achieved a maximum prevalence of 25.0% in June 2016.
source: This variant was first observed in April 2016 and achieved a maximum prevalence of 25.0% (CI953.8–46.2%) in June 2016 (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal prevalence data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The pfk13 C580Y variant was not identified in Region 1 between September 2016 and March 2017 despite constant malaria transmission.
source: Thereafter, it was not identified between September 2016 and March 2017 despite a constant transmission level of malaria in this region during this period.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal surveillance data.

claim: Pairwise nucleotide diversity (πsyn) in Guyana was 3.4 × 10−4, less than half the level observed in Southeast Asia (7.4 × 10−4) and nearly a third of that measured in Africa (1.0 × 10−3).
source: At synonymous sites within 4888 genes, pairwise nucleotide diversity (πsyn) in Guyana was 3.4 × 10−4, less than half the level observed in Southeast Asia (7.4 × 10−4) and nearly a third of that measured in Africa (1.0 × 10−3).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic diversity analysis comparing different geographic regions.

claim: Only one out of 46 Guyanese samples (2.2%) showed evidence of multiple parasite lineages (COI > 1).
source: In Guyana, 46 samples had sufficient sequencing coverage to assess their complexity of infection (COI), and only one (2.2%) showed evidence of multiple parasite lineages (COI > 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by complexity of infection analysis.

claim: Only 0.54% of wild-type Guyanese parasite pairs showed evidence of belonging to the same clonal lineage (IBD >0.75).
source: We found that only 0.54% of wild-type Guyanese parasite pairs showed evidence of belonging to the same clonal lineage (IBD >0.75).
evidence: The claim is supported by identity-by-descent analysis.

claim: Two P. falciparum isolates (O141-A and R086) from French Guiana were culture-adapted and genetically edited using a zinc-finger nuclease (ZFN) based approach.
source: To evaluate the impact of the pfk13 C580Y mutation on artemisinin susceptibility in parasites, we culture-adapted two P. falciparum isolates (O141-A and R086) from French Guiana (a neighboring country in the Guiana Shield) and genetically edited these lines using a previously described zinc-finger nuclease (ZFN) based approach (Straimer et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Both O141-A and R086 exhibit the pfcrt SVMNT haplotype associated with chloroquine resistance.
source: These two culture-adapted lines both exhibit the pfcrt SVMNT haplotype that is associated with chloroquine resistance, but only R086 carries the pfcrt C350R mutation that was earlier found to restore chloroquine susceptibility to South American parasites despite the presence of the SVMNT haplotype (Pelleau et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data and citation.

claim: Only R086 carries the pfcrt C350R mutation that restores chloroquine susceptibility to South American parasites despite the presence of the SVMNT haplotype.
source: These two culture-adapted lines both exhibit the pfcrt SVMNT haplotype that is associated with chloroquine resistance, but only R086 carries the pfcrt C350R mutation that was earlier found to restore chloroquine susceptibility to South American parasites despite the presence of the SVMNT haplotype (Pelleau et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data and citation.

claim: French Guianan parasite lines exhibit a high level of genomic similarity to genome-sequenced Guyanese parasites.
source: These parasite lines from French Guiana exhibit a high level of genomic similarity to our genome-sequenced Guyanese parasites (Figures 2c and d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic comparison data presented in figures.

claim: Introducing the pfk13 C580Y mutation caused a twenty-three fold increase in survival rate in R086 (0.6% ± 0.2 for R086 to 13.7% ± 1.5 for R086C580Y, p=0.006).
source: Introducing the pfk13 C580Y mutation caused a significant increase in the survival rate (twenty-three fold in R086: 0.6% ± 0.2 for R086 to 13.7% ± 1.5 for R086C580Y, p=0.006; fifty-five fold in O141-A: 0.5% ± 0.1 for O141-A compared to 27.6% ± 7.0 for O141-AC580Y, p=0.030, Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ring-stage Survival Assay data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Introducing the pfk13 C580Y mutation caused a fifty-five fold increase in survival rate in O141-A (0.5% ± 0.1 for O141-A compared to 27.6% ± 7.0 for O141-AC580Y, p=0.030).
source: Introducing the pfk13 C580Y mutation caused a significant increase in the survival rate (twenty-three fold in R086: 0.6% ± 0.2 for R086 to 13.7% ± 1.5 for R086C580Y, p=0.006; fifty-five fold in O141-A: 0.5% ± 0.1 for O141-A compared to 27.6% ± 7.0 for O141-AC580Y, p=0.030, Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ring-stage Survival Assay data presented in Figure 4.

claim: R086R539T showed a survival rate fifty-five times higher than the parental line (33.0% ± 5.0 compared to 0.6% ± 0.2, p=0.011).
source: R086R539T showed a survival rate fifty-five times higher than the parental line (33.0% ± 5.0 compared to 0.6% ± 0.2, p=0.011).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ring-stage Survival Assay data.

claim: Control assays found no significant difference in the survival rate of the parental vs. isogenic control lines.
source: Control assays found no significant difference in the survival rate of the parental vs. isogenic control lines (0.6% ± 0.2 for R086, 0.6% ± 0.4 for R086ctrlp=0.968, 0.5% ± 0.1 for O141-A and O141-Actrlp = 0.899) (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiment data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Pfk13 mutants showed a modest growth deficit compared to wild-type parent for both R086 and O141-A lines.
source: Results showed a modest growth deficit in pfk13 mutants compared to the wild-type parent for both the R086 and O141-A lines, suggesting that the pfk13 C580Y and R539T mutations negatively impact parasite growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by competitive growth assay data.

claim: Over 60 days, there was an 18% reduction in the frequency of the R539T mutant for the R086 line.
source: Over the 60 day period, we observed an 18% reduction in the frequency of the R539T mutant for the R086 line, and larger significant reductions of 24% and 40% in allele frequencies of the C580Y mutants of R086 and O141-A compared to their respective isogenic wild-type counterparts (Figure 5a, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by competitive growth assay data presented in Figure 5a.

claim: Over 60 days, there were reductions of 24% and 40% in allele frequencies of the C580Y mutants of R086 and O141-A compared to their respective isogenic wild-type counterparts.
source: Over the 60 day period, we observed an 18% reduction in the frequency of the R539T mutant for the R086 line, and larger significant reductions of 24% and 40% in allele frequencies of the C580Y mutants of R086 and O141-A compared to their respective isogenic wild-type counterparts (Figure 5a, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by competitive growth assay data presented in Figure 5a.

claim: The average reduced growth rate was −0.6%, −0.8% and −1.3% per 48 hr generation for R086R539T, R086C580Y and O141-AC580Y mutant lines, respectively, across 30 generations.
source: This reflected an average reduced growth rate of −0.6%, −0.8% and −1.3% per 48 hr generation of the R086R539T, R086C580Y and O141-AC580Y mutant lines, respectively, across 30 generations (Figure 5b, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by competitive growth assay data presented in Figure 5b.

claim: The C580Y mutation conferred a higher fitness cost compared to the R539T mutation.
source: In addition to observing that the C580Y mutation conferred a higher fitness cost compared to the R539T mutation, we also saw that the parasite genetic background contributed to the severity of the fitness deficit, as the growth defect in the C580Y mutation was substantially more pronounced in O141-A compared with R086 parasites (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the fitness costs of different mutations.

claim: The parasite genetic background contributed to the severity of the fitness deficit, as the growth defect in the C580Y mutation was substantially more pronounced in O141-A compared with R086 parasites.
source: In addition to observing that the C580Y mutation conferred a higher fitness cost compared to the R539T mutation, we also saw that the parasite genetic background contributed to the severity of the fitness deficit, as the growth defect in the C580Y mutation was substantially more pronounced in O141-A compared with R086 parasites (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing fitness costs in different genetic backgrounds.

claim: Pfk13 C580Y mutants have emerged independently in Guyana with an evolutionary origin distinct from Southeast Asia.
source: We report that mutant pfk13 has emerged independently in Guyana, with genome analysis indicating an evolutionary origin distinct from Southeast Asia.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing and haplotype analysis.

claim: Introducing pfk13 C580Y or R539T mutations by gene editing into local parasites conferred high levels of in vitro artemisinin resistance.
source: Introducing pfk13 C580Y or R539T mutations by gene editing into local parasites conferred high levels of in vitro artemisinin resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by Ring-stage Survival Assay data.

claim: In vitro growth competition assays revealed a fitness cost associated with pfk13 C580Y and R539T variants.
source: In vitro growth competition assays revealed a fitness cost associated with these pfk13 variants, potentially explaining why these resistance alleles have not increased in frequency more quickly in South America.
evidence: The claim is supported by competitive growth assay data.

claim: The fitness cost associated with pfk13 variants potentially explains why these resistance alleles have not increased in frequency more quickly in South America.
source: In vitro growth competition assays revealed a fitness cost associated with these pfk13 variants, potentially explaining why these resistance alleles have not increased in frequency more quickly in South America.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a hypothesis based on the observed fitness cost.

claim: Guyana was one of the first South American malaria-endemic countries to adopt and implement artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem) in 2004.
source: In 2004, Guyana was one of the first South American malaria-endemic countries to adopt and implement artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem), the current first-line therapy against P. falciparum.
evidence: The claim is stated as historical fact in the manuscript.

claim: In Western Cambodia, one C580Y lineage (KEL1) has displaced other mutations and has rapidly become the dominant pfk13 genotype (>80%).
source: In Western Cambodia, one C580Y linage (KEL1) has displaced other mutations and has rapidly become the dominant pfk13 genotype in that population (>80%) (Amato et al., 2018; Takala-Harrison et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: The KEL1 lineage has merged with a multicopy plasmepsin 2 and 3 lineage (PLA1) that is associated with piperaquine resistance.
source: This lineage has merged with a multicopy plasmepsin 2 and 3 lineage (PLA1) that is associated with piperaquine resistance (Amato et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Amato et al., 2018.

claim: In western Thailand at the border with Myanmar, a six-year period was required for distinct mutant pfk13 parasite lineages to collectively reach a population prevalence of 20%.
source: On the other side, in western Thailand, at the border with Myanmar, a six-year period was required for distinct mutant pfk13 parasite lineages to collectively reach a population prevalence of 20% (Amato et al., 2018; Anderson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: In western Thailand, a patchwork of pfk13 genotypes co-circulates and the prevalence of C580Y lineages fluctuates around 20–30%.
source: At the present time, a patchwork of pfk13 genotypes co-circulates in that population and the prevalence of C580Y lineages fluctuates around 20–30% (Kobasa et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kobasa et al., 2018.

claim: In Myanmar, the F446I mutation presently dominates the pfk13 mutant parasite population in certain sites and is associated with an intermediate resistance phenotype.
source: In Myanmar, pfk13 mutants are more diverse and the F446I mutation presently dominates the pfk13 mutant parasite population in certain sites, with this mutation being associated with an intermediate resistance phenotype (Han et al., 2020; Bonnington et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: In the Guiana Shield, lumefantrine remains a highly effective partner drug for artemisinin, and no mutations or phenotypes associated with lumefantrine resistance have been observed.
source: In the Guiana Shield, lumefantrine remains a highly effective partner drug for artemisinin, and no mutations or phenotypes associated with lumefantrine resistance have been observed (Legrand et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Legrand et al., 2012.

claim: High efficacy of the partner drug could be an important factor limiting the spread of pfk13 C580Y in Guyana.
source: High efficacy of the partner drug could therefore be an important factor limiting the spread of pfk13 C580Y in Guyana.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a hypothesis based on the effectiveness of lumefantrine.

claim: The P. falciparum population in South America is smaller and more recently established than in Southeast Asia.
source: Finally, both the low synonymous pairwise genetic diversity (πsyn = 3.4 x 10−4) and the low complexity of infection (COI, 2.2% of samples with a COI > 1) in Guyana are in keeping with the expectation that the P. falciparum population in South America is smaller and more recently established than in Southeast Asia (Yalcindag et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic diversity and complexity of infection data, supported by citation.

claim: Guyana has high outcrossing rates and few clonal lineages (0.54% pairs with IBD >0.75).
source: The present findings indicate high outcrossing rates and few clonal lineages in Guyana (0.54% pairs with IBD >0.75).
evidence: The claim is supported by identity-by-descent analysis.

claim: Clonal diversity may be greater in the Guiana Shield relative to the rest of South America.
source: These prior analyses used fewer genomic markers, but the results still suggest that clonal diversity may be greater in the Guiana Shield relative to the rest of the continent, possibly driven by the high P. falciparum transmission level observed in mining areas (Douine et al., 2016; Ministry of Public Health, 2018).
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from comparison with other South American studies.

claim: Haplotype richness may increase the likelihood that resistance mutations can successfully establish themselves in a permissive background.
source: As genomic background likely plays a key role in the persistence of resistance mutations like C580Y, this haplotype richness may increase the likelihood that resistance mutations can successfully establish themselves in a permissive background.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a hypothesis about the role of haplotype diversity.

claim: A low recombination rate may allow beneficial combinations to persist within the population.
source: Subsequently, a low recombination rate may allow these beneficial combinations to then persist within the population.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a hypothesis about recombination and persistence.

claim: The slower trajectory of pfk13 C580Y may be due to an impaired asexual blood-stage growth rate and the absence of compensatory mutations.
source: The slower trajectory of pfk13 C580Y may also be due to an impaired asexual blood-stage growth rate, and the absence of compensatory mutations that have been hypothesized to aid the spread of the C580Y mutation in Southeast Asia (Amato et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing hypotheses based on observed fitness costs and comparison with Southeast Asia.

claim: The C580Y mutation was associated with a more severe growth defect compared to the R539T mutation in asexual blood stage parasites.
source: Our data show that the C580Y mutation was associated with a more severe growth defect compared to the R539T mutation in these asexual blood stage parasites.
evidence: The claim is supported by competitive growth assay data.

claim: A similar fitness cost finding for C580Y was reported in C580Y-edited isolates from the Thailand-Myanmar border.
source: A similar finding was also recently reported in C580Y-edited isolates from the Thailand-Myanmar border (Nair et al., 2018), although disparate results were obtained for C580Y-edited isolates from Cambodia (Straimer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies showing different results.

claim: Disparate fitness cost results were obtained for C580Y-edited isolates from Cambodia.
source: A similar finding was also recently reported in C580Y-edited isolates from the Thailand-Myanmar border (Nair et al., 2018), although disparate results were obtained for C580Y-edited isolates from Cambodia (Straimer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Straimer et al., 2017.

claim: The contrasting fitness cost data underline the influence of the parasite's genomic background.
source: These contrasting data underline the influence of the parasite's genomic background, which potentially involves compensatory mutations that impact the overall growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing different study results.

claim: The WHO has categorized countries regarding artemisinin resistance based on pfk13 mutant prevalence and clinical response to artemisinin derivatives.
source: The World Health Organization (WHO) has categorized countries regarding artemisinin resistance based on pfk13 mutant prevalence and the clinical response to artemisinin derivatives (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization 2017 report.

claim: The WHO threshold of 5% pfk13 mutants has been met on several occasions in Guyana, first in 2010, then punctually in 2016–2017 in Region 1.
source: The threshold of 5% of pfk13 mutants has been met on several occasions in Guyana, first in 2010 (Chenet et al., 2016), then punctually in 2016–2017 in Region 1.
evidence: The claim is supported by prevalence data from the study and citation.

claim: Guyana has the status of suspected resistance to artemisinin derivatives according to WHO.
source: Nonetheless, in light of these findings, Guyana has the status of suspected resistance to artemisinin derivatives (World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization 2017 report.

claim: Pfk13 mutants are likely to expose the partner drug to the risk of emerging resistance.
source: Given their decreased susceptibility to DHA in vitro, these mutants are likely to expose the partner drug to the risk of emerging resistance.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferring risk based on in vitro resistance data.

claim: 854 P. falciparum isolates were collected in Guyana from March 2016 to September 2017 from febrile individuals visiting malaria clinics.
source: In collaboration with PAHO, 854 P. falciparum isolates were collected in Guyana from March 2016 to September 2017 in febrile individuals visiting the malaria clinic.
evidence: The claim describes the sample collection methods.

claim: Parasites came mainly from Region 1 (n = 114), 7 (n = 572) and 8 (n = 150) in Guyana.
source: Parasites associated with these samples came mainly from Region 1 (n = 114), 7 (n = 572) and 8 (n = 150) (Figure 1, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim describes the geographic distribution of samples.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing was performed on thirteen of the fourteen Guyana samples exhibiting the pfk13 C580Y mutation and 40 comparator samples with wild-type pfk13.
source: To understand the origin of the C580Y mutation and examine the genetic relatedness of the mutant strains, we performed whole-genome sequencing (WGS) on thirteen of the fourteen Guyana samples exhibiting the pfk13 C580Y mutation, as well as 40 comparator samples exhibiting wild-type pfk13 and collected at comparable locations and times.
evidence: The claim describes the whole-genome sequencing methods.

claim: Selective whole-genome amplification (SWGA) was performed on DNA samples to enrich parasite DNA prior to sequencing.
source: For the Guyana samples, we performed selective whole-genome amplification (SWGA) on DNA samples as previously described (Oyola et al., 2016) to enrich parasite DNA prior to sequencing on an Illumina HiSeqX instrument at the Broad Institute.
evidence: The claim describes the sequencing methods with citation.

claim: Reads were aligned to the P. falciparum v3 reference genome assembly using BWA-MEM.
source: We aligned reads to the P. falciparum v3 reference genome assembly using BWA-MEM (Li, 2013) and called SNPs and INDELs using the GATK HaplotypeCaller (Van der Auwera et al., 2013; McKenna et al., 2010; DePristo et al., 2011) according to the best practices for P. falciparum as determined by the Pf3K consortium (https://www.malariagen.net/projects/pf3k).
evidence: The claim describes the bioinformatics methods with citations.

claim: SNPs and INDELs were called using the GATK HaplotypeCaller according to Pf3K consortium best practices.
source: We aligned reads to the P. falciparum v3 reference genome assembly using BWA-MEM (Li, 2013) and called SNPs and INDELs using the GATK HaplotypeCaller (Van der Auwera et al., 2013; McKenna et al., 2010; DePristo et al., 2011) according to the best practices for P. falciparum as determined by the Pf3K consortium (https://www.malariagen.net/projects/pf3k).
evidence: The claim describes the bioinformatics methods with citations.

claim: Pairwise identity by descent (IBD) was calculated using a hidden Markov model (hmmIBD).
source: We calculated pairwise identity by descent (IBD) using a hidden Markov model (hmmIBD) (Schaffner et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim describes the analysis methods with citation.

claim: Complexity of infection was assessed using THE REAL McCOIL.
source: All genomic analyses were limited to samples containing only a single clonal lineage, as determined by THE REAL McCOIL (Chang et al., 2017) or as identified by the Pf3K consortium (Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim describes the analysis methods with citation.

claim: Ring-stage Survival Assays (RSA0-3h) were performed independently three times for each parasite line.
source: RSA0-3h were performed independently three times for each line.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: The pfk13 I543T-mutant IPC4912 strain (MRA1241) was used as an artemisinin-resistant control.
source: The pfk13 I543T-mutant IPC4912 strain (MRA1241) was used as an artemisinin-resistant control.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: Fitness assays were performed by inoculating an equal number of wild-type and mutant isogenic ring-stage parasites in a 6 ml culture at an initial parasitemia of 1%.
source: Fitness assays were performed by inoculating an equal number of wild-type and mutant isogenic ring-stage parasites in a 6 ml culture at an initial parasitemia of 1%.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: Each co-culture experiment was performed in duplicate on two independent occasions and monitored for 60 days.
source: Each co-culture experiment was performed in duplicate on two independent occasions and monitored for 60 days.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: The percentage of wild-type or mutant allele in each co-culture was determined using genomic DNA in a TaqMan Allelic Discrimination Real-Time PCR Assay.
source: The percentage of wild-type or mutant allele in each co-culture was determined using genomic DNA in a TaqMan Allelic Discrimination Real-Time PCR Assays.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: The TaqMan qPCR assay showed high efficiency (88–95%) and R2 values (0.98–1.00).
source: Robustness was demonstrated by high efficiency (88–95%) and R2 values (0.98–1.00) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a and b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by validation data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The TaqMan assay was able to accurately quantify different proportions of mutant alleles in pre-mixed samples.
source: Hence, our assay was able to accurately quantify the different proportions of the mutant alleles in these pre-mixed samples.
evidence: The claim is supported by validation experiments using pre-defined mixtures.

claim: 57.2% of genotyped samples outside the propeller domain were the 3D7 reference genotype.
source: We also genotyped the sequence outside of the propeller domain for 283 samples. Among these, 57.2% (CI9551.5–63.0%) were the 3D7 reference genotype, 42.0% (CI9536.3–47.8%) carried the pfk13 K189T mutation and 0.7% (CI950.0–1.7%) had a mixed genotype (wild-type/K189T).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data.

claim: 42.0% of genotyped samples outside the propeller domain carried the pfk13 K189T mutation.
source: We also genotyped the sequence outside of the propeller domain for 283 samples. Among these, 57.2% (CI9551.5–63.0%) were the 3D7 reference genotype, 42.0% (CI9536.3–47.8%) carried the pfk13 K189T mutation and 0.7% (CI950.0–1.7%) had a mixed genotype (wild-type/K189T).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data.

claim: 0.7% of genotyped samples outside the propeller domain had a mixed genotype (wild-type/K189T).
source: We also genotyped the sequence outside of the propeller domain for 283 samples. Among these, 57.2% (CI9551.5–63.0%) were the 3D7 reference genotype, 42.0% (CI9536.3–47.8%) carried the pfk13 K189T mutation and 0.7% (CI950.0–1.7%) had a mixed genotype (wild-type/K189T).
evidence: The claim is supported by genotyping data.

claim: Parasites from Guyana and French Guiana form a single cluster when compared with parasites from Africa.
source: (c) The parasites from Guyana and French Guiana form a single cluster when compared with parasites from Africa.
evidence: The claim is supported by principal components analysis presented in Figure 2c.

claim: The two edited parasite lines from French Guiana are highly similar to the sequenced parasite samples from Guyana including a pfk13 mutant.
source: (d) The two edited parasite lines from French Guiana are highly similar to the sequenced parasite samples from Guyana including a pfk13 mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by principal components analysis presented in Figure 2d.

claim: The median number of nucleotide differences between the two edited French Guianan lines and Guyanese parasites (0.23 per thousand nucleotides) is lower than the median nucleotide differences between parasite pairs drawn from within any of the other analyzed populations.
source: The median number of nucleotide differences between the two edited French Guianan lines and Guyanese parasites (FrGu-Guy; 0.23 per thousand nucleotides) is lower than the median nucleotide differences between parasite pairs drawn from within any of the other analyzed populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic comparison data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
